Chapter 8: The Flywheel and the Doom Loop—Building and Sustaining Momentum.
Let’s take a closer look at this powerful idea.
One thing that really stands out on the journey from good to great is that lasting change isn’t some overnight miracle. It’s more like a steady climb—one step at a time, building on each small win. Imagine you’re pushing a huge, heavy flywheel. At first, it barely budges. Every push feels like it’s going nowhere. But you keep at it, push after push, and slowly, that wheel starts to move. A little faster each time. And then, something amazing happens—the momentum takes over, and the wheel almost spins on its own.
That’s what’s called the flywheel effect. It’s simple, but honestly, it’s pretty profound. Great organizations don’t become successful through one big, dramatic event. Instead, they stick to consistent, focused effort, day after day. Over time, all those small actions add up, and suddenly, they’re achieving results that look like breakthroughs. But really, it’s years of persistence paying off.
Now, let’s talk about the other side—the doom loop. Some organizations fall into this trap. Instead of building steady momentum, they’re always looking for the next quick fix. They jump from one program or shiny new idea to another, hoping for instant results. But every time they switch direction, they disrupt the progress they’ve made. Trust starts to erode. Motivation drops off. And it gets harder and harder to actually make real progress.
Here’s what makes the difference:
The flywheel is all about steady, cumulative progress—each step building on the last, momentum growing as you go. The doom loop, on the other hand, is full of quick shifts, inconsistency, and lost trust.
Think about a company you’ve seen rise to the top. From the outside, it might look like an overnight success. But if you talk to the people inside, they’ll tell you it was years of patient, disciplined work. That’s the flywheel in action.
So, how do you actually build and keep that momentum going?
First, commit to a clear direction, and stick with it—even when it feels like progress is slow. Celebrate the small wins, and recognize every step forward. Avoid the urge to chase after every new fad or abandon your strategy if results don’t come instantly. And maybe most important, nurture a culture of patience, resilience, and long-term thinking.
When you embrace the flywheel approach, you’re setting yourself up for breakthroughs that really last. And the best part? You’re creating a foundation that others can build on long after you’re gone.
